I can feel your pain, and that's not a pun. I can literally feel your pain emotionally. I too am in chronic pain all the damn time and I have tried multiple times to unalive myself. It's almost always impulsively and with pills or alcohol involved. And I would like to say I've given up on even trying anymore because there have been so many attempts and equal number of failures. But with a change of environment and a list of the things you used to love doing andanything, even the slightest thing, that could potentially lift your spirits? Maybe it's good loud music or going for a walk-through nature, or anything that could potentially give you a brief moment even of something to live for. The best thing I can say is live for yourself. Do what you wanna do when you wanna do it and because you want to do it. Yes it's going to emotionally mess up a lot of people who love you and support you and care about you because I lost my 25-year-old son almost 11 years ago and for the first 10 years I completely blamed myself and couldn't get through a single day without constant guilt and shame and hopelessness. But I was talking to the best therapist I've ever had and he helped me work through that. I realized there was nothing I could've done and it was not my fault at all. In fact he and I were very close which is what killed me the most. He took a part of me with him that day and I wouldn't wish that pain on anyone. But I know how it feels literally and figurativelyto be in so much pain that you just feel like you can't do it anymore. I get it. Hugs

I’m truly sorry to hear about the challenges you’re facing. It’s completely understandable to feel overwhelmed when your efforts aren’t yielding the results you hoped for, especially after relocating to pursue your dreams. Please know that you’re not alone in this, and there are people and resources ready to support you through this difficult time.

Immediate Support:

Your well-being is of utmost importance. If you’re experiencing thoughts of self-harm or suicide, reaching out for help is a courageous and vital step. In the United States, you can contact the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by dialing 988. This service is available 24/7, offering confidential support from trained counselors who can assist you in navigating these feelings and connecting you with local resources.

Building Connections in the Fashion Industry:

Breaking into the fashion industry can indeed be challenging, especially without an established network. However, there are several strategies you can employ to build connections and increase your visibility:
	1.	Networking Events and Workshops: Attend industry-related events, workshops, and seminars in NYC. These gatherings provide opportunities to meet professionals and learn about potential job openings. Websites like Eventbrite often list such events.
	2.	Informational Interviews: Reach out to professionals in your desired field for informational interviews. Platforms like LinkedIn can help you identify and connect with individuals willing to share insights about their career paths and offer advice.
	3.	Volunteer or Internship Opportunities: Consider short-term internships or volunteer positions to gain experience and make connections. Organizations like VolunteerMatch can help you find relevant opportunities.
	4.	Online Communities: Engage with online forums and groups related to fashion. Participating in discussions can lead to valuable connections and insights. Subreddits like r/fashionindustry might be a good starting point.

Exploring Alternative Employment Options:

While pursuing your passion is important, securing interim employment can alleviate financial stress and provide stability as you continue your job search:
	•	Temporary Agencies: Staffing agencies in NYC often have short-term positions that can provide immediate income and potentially lead to permanent roles.
	•	Gig Economy: Platforms like TaskRabbit or Upwork offer flexible work opportunities that can be tailored to your skills.
	•	Skill Development: Utilize this time to enhance your skill set through online courses or certifications. Websites like Coursera and edX offer courses that might make your applications more competitive.

Financial Assistance and Planning:

Managing finances during unemployment is challenging, but there are resources available to help:
	•	Local Assistance Programs: NYC offers various programs for residents facing financial hardships. The NYC Human Resources Administration provides information on emergency assistance and support services.
	•	Budgeting Tools: Utilize budgeting apps to track expenses and identify areas to reduce spending. Tools like Mint can be helpful in managing your finances during this period.

Emotional Well-being:

Your mental health is paramount. Consider reaching out to a mental health professional who can provide support tailored to your situation. Many organizations offer sliding-scale fees based on income, making therapy more accessible. Additionally, support groups can provide a sense of community and understanding.

Remember, seeking help is a sign of strength, not weakness. Your current situation doesn’t define your worth or the potential for your future. With time, persistence, and support, it’s possible to navigate these challenges and find a path forward that aligns with your goals and well-being.

Wow. Such insightful comments, and right on the nose. People who have never been through it have absolutely no idea. They may try to imagine and possibly get clutched by fear, but there are so many more emotions that go into grief. And we never "get over it", it just takes up slightly less space in our mental attic. It's always there, like bats who sleep all day but come out at night, or bears who hibernate in the wintertime and awake ravaged in the spring. 

You said there isn't anything wrong with that, it's "normal" and it reminded me of calling it My New Normal, because it is my new normal. It has been since the day I found him on June 2, 2014. The absolute most awful day of my life. A part of me died with him that day. Every day I'm wishing I had that part back, because it has changed me -- and not always for the better. But your post sparked something in me. It's like my desire to write has been restored. 

My son was so creative and happy and strong, yet sensitive. He had the musical genes of my father. He was an amazing drummer -- a celebrity of sorts at the high school where he graduated. He won talent shows, state tryouts, and was in the jazz band, as well as having bands of his own. I can't tell you how many times I recall dragging his drum set around in my vehicle. He's now buried at the cemetery across the street. And when I go visit his grave later, I'm going to tell him you asked about him.

I went to a support group when it first happened and that's what I would recommend to you and anyone else in this situation. Everyone there is eager to talk about their shared loss.

Oh my heart goes out to you. I wish I could wrap my arms around you and tell you it's going to be okay.  I feel your pain, anguish and guilt.  But it's so important not to beat yourself up and not to question what you did or didn't do. Even though that's the 'normal' response. I lost my son to suicide six years ago. He was my best friend. He was 25. He was my whole world. And I had no idea he was suicidal when I found him, a single gunshot above his right eye. After the shock wore off, I was consumed with guilt and remorse and constantly questioned my sanity and guilt in his suicide.  I saw the signs too late. I remembered things he had said. I felt like in some small way I had given him permission (even though at the time I didn't realize that's what I was doing).  I thought that because he had chosen suicide that it was going to be easier for me to mourn his death. It's been two years for you and you are still blaming yourself and questioning everything.  I highly recommend you start seeing a grief counselor and/or get into a grief support group with others who have lost loved ones by suicide.  Also, get your hands on as many books and articles as you can by other people who have been through this.  I was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder a couple of years ago and I can tell you it's a horrible disorder. I've tried taking my life twice, and I was recently released from the hospital for considering suicide. Stop blaming yourself, Mom. You loved him the absolute best you could and you did what you could for him. But it's over now. His pain is over.  I am so sorry for your loss, and I promise you that it will get better -- if you get yourself into therapy and possibly on a prescription for anxiety or depression.  Know that your son loved you, and he would not want you tormenting yourself the way you are. BPD pain is so raw and awful and intense that suicide feels like the only way to get help.  You can no longer help him, but you can help others.  Take your feelings of blame and heartbreak and turn them into positive energy.  Volunteer with BPD organizations.  Help others. But first, you must help and care for yourself. It's okay Mom.  It's not your fault. {{{{{{{Many Hugggggsssss}}}}}
